brief: one turnstile at Atlantic Terminal admits a passenger who has not been alive since 1974, every weekday, at 7:52, and the system logs it faithfully and the maintenance crew has stopped filing the report and started nodding, and the woman it lets through is dressed for an office that was demolished forty years ago and is never late

name: The Watched Watching Back
brief: a Sunset Park teenager builds a rig from parts that watches the watchers, and her wall of screens shows every lens on her block from the lens's own angle, and what she discovers and cannot stop thinking about is how boring it is, hours of nothing, a cat, a leaf, an old man sitting down, and she starts leaving small beautiful things in frame for whoever is on the other end

name: The Consent Form Bloom
brief: the terms of service have physicalized and grow across the city as a fast climbing vine, and a Jackson Heights tenant organizer walks her block with shears cutting it back off doorways and strollers and one sleeping man, and she has read every clause, all of it, the only person in New York who has, and she does not sleep much

name: The Surveillance Quilt
brief: a Harlem quilting circle has been piecing the watching into cloth for a decade, one square per camera installed on their avenue, and the quilt is now forty feet long and hangs from the community center at the summer block party, and it is beautiful, and that is the argument, that the record of being watched belongs to the watched

name: The Building That Refused to Testify
brief: subpoenaed for its footage, a Grand Concourse building simply declines, its cameras all turning to face the sky in unison at 3 a.m. and staying there, and the super swears he did not touch them, and the tenants organize around the building the way you would around an elder, and the footage of the night in question shows six hours of clouds

name: The Face Blur Vigilante
brief: he moves through crowds smearing faces out of the record with a device the size of a lighter, protecting people who never learn they were protected, and his own face is the only one he cannot blur, and so he is the most photographed unknown man in the city, and he accepts this as the tax, eye flowers opening in the blurred wake

name: The Cloud Storage Cemetery
brief: under a Queens data hall the dead are kept as footage, every recorded moment of them, and a night technician has become their unofficial keeper, playing back short clips into the empty aisles so that somebody is watching, which he considers the entire job, and the hum of the racks in there is famously, unaccountably warm

name: The Prayer That Jams the Signal
brief: during maghrib on a Bay Ridge block every device within four hundred feet goes quiet, and it has happened daily for years and no engineer has explained it, and the imam declines to comment except to say that some things are simply between you and God, and the block has grown fond of the fifteen minutes of silence and now schedules its arguments around it

name: The Audit of Small Sins
brief: the system publishes its findings on one Staten Island cul de sac, and the sins are all tiny, a bag in the wrong bin, a borrowed hose, a lie about a casserole, and the neighbors, expecting horror, find the list so mundane and so human that they print it and laugh and then, unexpectedly, forgive each other things that predate the cameras by thirty years

name: The Night the Cameras Looked Away
brief: for one night every lens in New York turns to face the harbor at the same moment, and the city goes about its business entirely unobserved, and what people do with the privacy is almost nothing dramatic, they sit closer, they say the thing, they cry in public, and the harbor, being watched by all of it, holds very still, eye flowers opening across the turned lenses

name: The Pneumatic Bodega Line
brief: brass tubes run under Washington Heights connecting every bodega on the hill, and the network moves a loosie, a lime, a spare key, a plate of food for somebody's mother, at ninety miles an hour, and the dispatcher is a fifteen year old who knows the whole grid by feel and has never once misrouted a plate, and the tubes make a sound the block finds soothing, eye flowers opening at the brass junctions

name: The Stoop to Stoop Zipline Union
brief: Bed Stuy runs on ziplines strung roofline to stoop, and the union that maintains them is four retired ironworkers and a teenager with a harness, and the rules are posted nowhere and known by everyone, groceries yes, arguments no, and the fastest run in the borough is a nine year old going stoop to stoop in four seconds flat with a birthday cake held perfectly level

name: The Sideways Elevator Conductor
brief: in a midtown tower the elevators travel sideways as well as up, and the conductor who runs car six has mapped routes nobody else knows, taking a heartbroken paralegal on the long way around the forty second floor past nine windows of sunset, and charging her nothing, and telling her the car does that on its own sometimes

name: The Folded Subway Engineer
brief: she has learned to fold the tunnel, bringing Far Rockaway within four minutes of Inwood by pinching the line, and the ride passes through a corridor of impossible geometry where the windows show both ends of the city at once, and she does it only for the last train, only for the people who have been up too long, and the transit authority has no idea

name: The Rooftop Gondola of Sunset Park
brief: cable cars run roof to roof over Fifth Avenue from the Chinese groceries to the Mexican bakeries to the Ecuadorian church, and the operator is a Palestinian grandfather who has learned the greeting in eleven languages and uses all of them every single trip, and the gondola makes the crossing in ninety seconds and the neighborhood in about a generation, eye flowers opening along the cable

name: The E-Bike Murmuration
brief: four hundred delivery riders leave the Elmhurst staging lot at once and move as a single organism, splitting around a bus and reforming, and the rider at the head tonight is a Malian man three months in the city who does not yet have the language and does not need it, because the flock speaks in shoulders, and the murmuration is the most beautiful thing on Queens Boulevard and nobody who is not in it ever notices

name: The Tidal Commuter
brief: he rides the East River tide to work, stepping in at Hallets Point at slack water and stepping out at Wall Street exactly on the turn, and the river carries him because he has learned to ask correctly, and he is the only man in finance who arrives smelling of salt and is the only one they never argue with, eye flowers opening in his wake

name: The Steam Pipe Riders
brief: kids ride the steam under the streets, borne up on the pressure like paper on a fan, popping out of orange and white stacks at 14th and Bleecker and Union Square, and the steam crew know all their faces and have never once reported it, and instead have quietly recalibrated the pressure at three intersections to make the landings softer

name: The Escalator That Goes Somewhere Else
brief: the up escalator at one Bronx station arrives at a different Bronx, greener, with the elevated line still there and running, and a woman rides it every Sunday to visit a candy store demolished in 1988, and buys the same thing, and comes back down with it, and it is real, and it is always still warm

name: The Manhole Paratrooper
brief: he drops into the sewers as easily as other people take stairs, and comes up wherever he needs to be, and the network he uses is not the sewers exactly but a thing that lives alongside them, and he moves packages for a network of grandmothers across four boroughs, medicine mostly, and has never been late and has never explained himself

name: The Water Taxi That Flies
brief: a harbor taxi lifts off the chop at full throttle and simply keeps rising, running a route over Governors Island at two hundred feet, and the captain is a Trinidadian woman who treats the flying part as unremarkable and the ferry schedule as sacred, and she has never been a minute late in either medium

name: The Grand Central Wormhole Clerk
brief: behind the information booth is a second booth, and the clerk there sells tickets to places the timetable does not list, a Tuesday in 1961, the Bronx your mother described, the version of this station with the old ceiling, and the fare is always something you would rather not part with, and everybody pays it, eye flowers opening around the brass clock

name: The Skateboard That Rides Sound
brief: a Ridgewood kid rides the sound of the city itself, dropping into the roar of the M train, carving the bass of a passing car, and the ride is only as good as the block is loud, and on quiet streets she has to walk, and her favorite line in the whole city is Roosevelt Avenue under the 7 at rush hour, which she describes as a wave that never closes out

name: The Sidewalk That Moves for the Elderly
brief: one Brighton Beach block's concrete has begun quietly conveying its oldest residents, carrying them the last hundred feet to the door, slowing at the curb, and the young people do not feel it at all, and the old people have agreed among themselves not to mention it in case it stops, and they arrive home each day slightly less tired than they should be

name: The Cargo Bike Caravan of Corona
brief: thirty cargo bikes leave the Corona market before dawn stacked with plantains and flowers and one entire mattress, and the caravan moves as a single articulated animal through Queens, and the woman at the front has been leading it for twenty two years and knows every pothole by its first name, eye flowers opening in the flower load

name: The Fire Escape Funicular
brief: a Chinatown tenement's fire escape runs like a funicular, hauling groceries and grandmothers and a whole tea service to the sixth floor on a counterweight of bricks, and the engineering is entirely unlicensed and entirely sound, having been designed by a retired machinist on the third floor who will not accept thanks, only tangerines

name: The Bus That Waits for You Specifically
brief: the B41 has begun waiting, holding at the stop with the doors open until the specific person who needs it arrives, sometimes two minutes, sometimes eleven, and the ridership has stopped complaining because everyone has now been the person, and the driver denies everything and keeps a hand on the door

name: The Ferry of Second Chances
brief: the last boat of the night runs a route that is not on any schedule, and everyone aboard is going back to a decision, and the crossing takes exactly as long as the person needs, and the deckhand who works it, a young man from St George, has watched a thousand people stand at the rail and turn around, and he has never once taken the trip himself

name: The Pothole Portal Inspector
brief: she inspects the potholes that are not potholes, the ones that open onto other parts of the city, and she carries cones and a clipboard and the authority of nobody, and today's is on Atlantic Avenue and drops directly into a Rockaway summer of some year she declines to specify, and she cones it off and sits beside it until dusk, letting the warm air out

name: The Rockaway Surf Train
brief: the A train comes out of the tunnel and keeps going into the water, and the surfers ride it out past the break and step off the last car into the swell, boards under arms, and the conductor gives them the horn, and the train circles back through the shallows for the ones coming in, salt on the windows, eye flowers opening on the wet steel

name: The Ladder Between Boroughs
brief: a wooden ladder leans against nothing at the Queens end of the Pulaski and reaches the Brooklyn end, and it is thirty feet long and spans a mile, and the man who owns it has run a ferry service on it for years, one at a time, no questions, and he holds the bottom, and he has never had a fall

name: The Bridge That Shortcuts
brief: the Manhattan Bridge, tired of the traffic, begins offering a shortcut, a fold in the middle for anyone who really needs it, and a woman driving her father to a hospital in Brooklyn takes it without thinking and arrives before she left, and the bridge does not do it again for her, and she understands why, eye flowers opening in the fold

name: The Elevator Operator of the Empty Shaft
brief: in a Tribeca cast iron building the shaft has no car and he operates it anyway, standing in the opening in full uniform, and people step in and arrive where they intended, and the freight of the thing is his absolute conviction, and the day he calls in sick the shaft is simply a hole and two people nearly walk into it

name: The Light Horse of Central Park
brief: the carriage horse is made of light now and does not tire and does not mind, and the driver, third generation, has mixed feelings he articulates to nobody, and at the end of the shift he still brushes it down, out of habit, and the light moves under the brush like a real coat, eye flowers opening in the mane

name: The Last Mile Angels
brief: the final hundred feet of every delivery in the city is handled by whoever is closest, a kid, a super, a woman with a walker, an entire informal relay that has never been organized and has never failed, and tonight a hot bag crosses six pairs of hands in a Gowanus stairwell and arrives upstairs faster than any professional could manage it

name: The Canal Street Impossible Electronics
brief: the table under the scaffolding sells devices that should not exist, a remote that pauses one specific argument, a charger that runs on being thanked, a speaker that only plays what the room needs, and the vendor tests each one on a customer before selling it and refuses the sale about half the time, saying, this is not for you, come back in a year

name: The Umbrella That Argues With Rain
brief: invented in a Ditmas Park basement, the umbrella negotiates rather than blocks, and rain that has been reasoned with falls politely around the user, and the inventor cannot mass produce it because every unit must be taught to argue in the dialect of the specific weather over the specific block, which he does, personally, one at a time

name: The Radiator Whisperer's Wrench
brief: a super in Inwood carries a wrench that translates the knocking, and the pipes in his six buildings are the only ones in New York that get answered, and what they mostly want, he reports, is to be told the season is nearly over, and he tells them, and they quiet down, and the tenants think he is a magician, eye flowers opening on the pipe

name: The Keychain That Holds a Room
brief: she carries a keychain with one extra key that opens a room she keeps in her pocket, a small warm room with a chair and a window onto her mother's kitchen, and she has let four people into it in her life, and the fifth is a stranger on the 6 train having the worst night of her life, and she hands over the key without a word

name: The Fan That Blows August Backward
brief: a Fort Greene window fan runs in reverse and pushes the heat back into July, and the block has one, shared, moved apartment to apartment on a schedule enforced by a committee of grandmothers, and by Labor Day the summer has been thoroughly redistributed and everybody has had a fair share of the good part

name: The MetroCard That Remembers
brief: a worn card in a Bay Ridge wallet holds every ride the owner ever took, and swiped at the right station it plays one back, and today it plays her first day in the city, 1996, arriving alone at Ditmars with two bags, and the woman it plays for stands at the turnstile in the middle of rush hour and lets the crowd go around her

name: The Ghost Pepper Translator
brief: a Jackson Heights cook has built a device that turns heat into meaning, and one bite of what she serves conveys the entire argument her grandmother could never win in English, and diners come out of the restaurant changed and slightly sweating, and the device is a clay pot and a spoon and forty years of practice

name: The Laundromat Time Machine
brief: the third dryer from the left in a Bushwick laundromat returns clothes from other times, a jacket you lost in 2011, a child's sock from a child now grown, and the owner has posted no notice and simply lets people find out, and sits behind the counter watching them hold things they had stopped looking for

name: The Inventor of the Rent Meter
brief: in a Mott Haven workshop stacked to the ceiling with salvage a woman has built the rent meter, a brass instrument that measures what a block is actually worth in the only units that matter, funerals attended, kids raised, doors held, meals brought upstairs, and it reads high everywhere the market reads low, and she has bolted one to the front of her building where the whole street can watch the needle sit at the top of the dial, and the developers who come to look leave without saying anything, watcher lattice and data lace worked through the brass, eye flowers opening across the instrument face

name: The Bodega Cat Collar Interface
brief: the cat wears a collar that translates, and what the cat has to say about the neighborhood turns out to be extensive, precise and largely correct, and the owner has begun consulting it on hiring, and business has improved, and the cat has requested and received a better chair, eye flowers opening in the collar

name: The Nail Salon Nanotech
brief: in Flushing the technicians work at a scale below sight, and the manicure they give holds a small program, one that makes the wearer's hands slightly luckier for two weeks, and the price is the same as everywhere else, and the waitlist is not, and the owner is entirely uninterested in scaling it up

name: The Sneaker That Maps the City
brief: a Harlem kid's sneakers draw the city as he walks it, the sole leaving a line only he can see, and after four years the map behind him is the most accurate document of a life in New York ever produced, and it shows, clearly, the block he never leaves and the one route out of it he has walked eleven thousand times

name: The Radio That Plays the Block
brief: a Bronx radio picks up the block itself, tuned between stations, and what comes through is the sound of every apartment at once, layered into something like music, and the man who built it listens to it more than anything else and describes it, accurately, as the best station in the city with no advertising

name: The Deli Slicer of Fine Distinctions
brief: the slicer at a Greenpoint deli cuts things other than meat, and the counterman uses it on the differences people bring in, the gap between what was said and what was meant, and he can shave that so thin you can see through it, and he wraps it in white paper and hands it over and nobody has ever asked for money back

name: The Weather Merchant of Sheepshead Bay
brief: his window unit does not cool the room, it sells the room's weather to whoever needs it, and he moves August out of an overheated apartment and into a February kitchen four blocks away, and the ledger of who owes whom which season is kept entirely in his head and has never been disputed

name: The Stoop Speaker of Perfect Volume
brief: the speaker on a Sunset Park stoop plays at exactly the volume each listener needs, loud for the dancing and inaudible to the baby upstairs and just right for the old man who is pretending not to enjoy it, and the block has never once had the police called, and no engineer has been able to reproduce it, eye flowers opening from the grille

name: The Recipe Printer
brief: a machine in an Astoria kitchen prints food from memory rather than instruction, and a Greek grandmother feeds it her recollection of her mother's cooking and it produces, imperfectly, exactly what she remembers rather than what was ever actually made, and she says this is better, and she is right

name: The Pigeon Post Uplink
brief: the Bushwick loft keeper has bonded his birds to the network, and they carry what the network cannot, messages too heavy to be trusted to it, and the birds go out at dawn over the whole city and come back with their small precious weight, and he has never lost one, and he can name all sixty

name: The Window Unit Oracle
brief: the air conditioner in a Rego Park bedroom answers questions, one per summer, in the rattle of its compressor, and the family has learned to save the question, and this year the daughter is going to ask about leaving, and the whole family knows it, and nobody has said anything, and the unit is dripping onto the sill the way it always has

name: The Repair Cafe of Impossible Objects
brief: every Saturday in a Kensington church basement people bring what cannot be fixed, a marriage, a knee, a lamp from a demolished house, and the volunteers try anyway, and the success rate on lamps is excellent and on the rest is not, and everybody comes back, and the tea is good, eye flowers opening among the parts

name: The Battery That Runs on Argument
brief: two Fordham Road brothers have been arguing since 1979 and a neighbor has finally tapped it, and the building runs entirely on their disagreement about a car neither of them owns anymore, and the lights dim slightly when they are getting along, which the block finds a reasonable trade

name: The Toolbelt of the Sidewalk Surgeon
brief: she repairs the street itself, curbs and hydrants and one collapsed corner of Nostrand Avenue, working with tools that do not exist in any catalogue, and the city has no record of her and the block has a shrine to her, and the corner she fixed has not cracked in eleven winters

name: The Phone That Only Calls Home
brief: found in a Ridgewood junk shop, the phone connects to exactly one place, and for every person who picks it up that place is different, and it is always the number you would call if you still could, and the shop owner has arranged three chairs around it and charges nothing and looks away while people talk

name: The Mirror That Shows the Neighborhood
brief: the mirror in a Crown Heights barbershop shows not the customer but the block behind them across forty years, and you sit down for a fade and watch the storefronts change and change back, and the barber has stopped explaining it and simply lets the chair do its work, eye flowers opening around the frame

name: The Vending Machine of Last Resorts
brief: in a Port Authority corridor a machine dispenses exactly one thing to each person and it is never what they selected and always what they needed, a MetroCard, a phone number, a sandwich, an address in Elmhurst where someone will take them in, and it takes whatever coins you have, including none
